```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)

orders <- read_csv("data/orders.csv")
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv")
products <- read_csv("data/products.csv")
sellers <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv")
```

## The dataset

This project uses four e-commerce datasets:

- orders
- order items
- products
- sellers

Together, these datasets provide information about fulfillment, seller location, freight cost, product price, and product characteristics.

## Original dataset dimensions

Before cleaning or joining the data, I first checked the size of each dataset.

```{r}
original_dimensions <- tibble(
  dataset = c(
    "Orders",
    "Order Items",
    "Products",
    "Sellers"
  ),
  rows = c(
    nrow(orders),
    nrow(order_items),
    nrow(products),
    nrow(sellers)
  ),
  columns = c(
    ncol(orders),
    ncol(order_items),
    ncol(products),
    ncol(sellers)
  )
)

original_dimensions
```

The orders table contains one row per order, while the order-items table can contain multiple rows for the same order because one order may contain several products.

## Data structure

I reviewed the structure of each dataset to understand the available variables and their data types.

### Orders

```{r}
glimpse(orders)
```

The orders dataset contains order status, purchase dates, delivery dates, delivery duration, and estimated delivery duration.

### Order items

```{r}
glimpse(order_items)
```

The order-items dataset connects orders with products and sellers and includes product price and freight value.

### Products

```{r}
glimpse(products)
```

The products dataset contains product category information and physical characteristics such as weight, length, height, and width.

### Sellers

```{r}
glimpse(sellers)
```

The sellers dataset provides seller location information including seller city and state.

## Missing values

Before deciding how to clean the data, I checked how many missing values appear in each dataset.

```{r}
missing_summary <- tibble(
  dataset = c(
    "Orders",
    "Order Items",
    "Products",
    "Sellers"
  ),
  missing_values = c(
    sum(is.na(orders)),
    sum(is.na(order_items)),
    sum(is.na(products)),
    sum(is.na(sellers))
  )
)

missing_summary
```

The orders and products datasets contain missing values, so I looked more closely at which variables are affected.

### Missing values in orders

```{r}
orders_missing <- tibble(
  variable = names(orders),
  missing_values = colSums(is.na(orders))
) |>
  filter(missing_values > 0)

orders_missing
```

The missing values in the orders dataset affect delivery information.

Because this project evaluates fulfillment performance, orders without a usable delivery duration cannot be included in the delivery analysis.

### Missing values in products

```{r}
products_missing <- tibble(
  variable = names(products),
  missing_values = colSums(is.na(products))
) |>
  filter(missing_values > 0)

products_missing
```

Some product category, description, and physical-characteristic fields contain missing values.

These records are retained because those variables are not required for every part of the analysis.

For analyses involving product weight, records with missing product weight are excluded only from that specific analysis rather than from the full dataset.

## Duplicate rows

I also checked for complete duplicate rows in each original dataset.

```{r}
duplicate_summary <- tibble(
  dataset = c(
    "Orders",
    "Order Items",
    "Products",
    "Sellers"
  ),
  duplicate_rows = c(
    sum(duplicated(orders)),
    sum(duplicated(order_items)),
    sum(duplicated(products)),
    sum(duplicated(sellers))
  )
)

duplicate_summary
```

No complete duplicate rows were found in the four source datasets.

Therefore, no records needed to be removed because of complete duplication.

## Cleaning the order data

The analysis focuses on completed deliveries.

I therefore kept only orders with a delivered status and a non-missing delivery duration.

```{r}
orders_clean <- orders |>
  filter(order_status == "delivered") |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days))
```

The effect of this cleaning decision is shown below.

```{r}
cleaning_summary <- tibble(
  stage = c(
    "Original Orders",
    "Cleaned Delivered Orders"
  ),
  rows = c(
    nrow(orders),
    nrow(orders_clean)
  ),
  columns = c(
    ncol(orders),
    ncol(orders_clean)
  )
)

cleaning_summary
```

This cleaning step removed **`r nrow(orders) - nrow(orders_clean)` rows** from the original orders dataset.

These rows were excluded because the analysis focuses on completed orders with a usable delivery duration.

Keeping them would prevent a consistent comparison between actual delivery duration and estimated delivery duration.

## Creating delivery status

A delivery-performance variable is created by comparing actual delivery duration with estimated delivery duration.

```{r}
orders_clean <- orders_clean |>
  mutate(
    delivery_status = if_else(
      delivery_days <= estimated_days,
      "On Time",
      "Late"
    )
  )
```

I then checked how many cleaned orders fall into each delivery category.

```{r}
delivery_status_summary <- orders_clean |>
  count(delivery_status) |>
  mutate(
    percent = n / sum(n) * 100
  )

delivery_status_summary
```

This variable gives the analysis a consistent way to compare delivery reliability across seller groups.

## Building the analytical dataset

The cleaned order data is then joined with order-item, seller, and product information.

```{r}
supply_chain_data <- orders_clean |>
  left_join(
    order_items,
    by = "order_id"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    sellers,
    by = "seller_id"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    products,
    by = "product_id"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    freight_ratio = freight_value / price
  )
```

I created `supply_chain_data` so the main supply-chain variables are available in one table.

This allows delivery performance, seller location, freight cost, product price, and product characteristics to be analyzed together.

## Final dataset dimensions

After cleaning, joining, and creating the freight-to-price ratio, I checked the dimensions of the analytical dataset.

```{r}
final_dimensions <- tibble(
  dataset = c(
    "Cleaned Orders",
    "Final Supply Chain Dataset"
  ),
  rows = c(
    nrow(orders_clean),
    nrow(supply_chain_data)
  ),
  columns = c(
    ncol(orders_clean),
    ncol(supply_chain_data)
  )
)

final_dimensions
```

The final analytical dataset contains more rows than the cleaned orders dataset because one order can contain multiple items.

This means the final dataset is analyzed at the **order-item level**, while the cleaned orders dataset contains one row per order.

## Final dataset structure

I reviewed the final analytical dataset to confirm that the expected fulfillment, seller, freight, price, and product variables are available.

```{r}
glimpse(supply_chain_data)
```

The final dataset combines fulfillment, seller, freight, price, and product information in one analytical table.

## Freight-to-price ratio

Freight cost alone does not show how large the shipping cost is relative to the value of the product.

For example, the same freight charge can represent a small portion of an expensive product's value but a large portion of a lower-priced product's value.

The `freight_ratio` variable was therefore created as:

```text
freight value / product price
```

I checked its distribution before using it in the exploration.

```{r}
freight_ratio_summary <- supply_chain_data |>
  summarise(
    minimum = min(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    average = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum = max(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

freight_ratio_summary
```

The large difference between the median and maximum shows that some products have unusually high freight costs relative to their price.

I did not automatically remove these observations because they may represent real costly shipments that are relevant to the business question.

Instead, their effect is examined during the exploratory analysis.

## Variables used in the exploration

The main variables used in the Exploration page are:

- `seller_state` — seller location
- `delivery_days` — actual delivery duration
- `estimated_days` — estimated delivery duration
- `delivery_status` — on-time or late delivery
- `purchase_year` — purchase year
- `purchase_month` — purchase month
- `price` — product selling price
- `freight_value` — freight cost
- `freight_ratio` — freight cost relative to product price
- `product_weight_g` — product weight
- `seller_id` — seller identifier
- `order_id` — order identifier

These variables provide the information needed to compare seller scale, delivery reliability, freight burden, marketplace activity over time, and product-related shipping costs.
